title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting nonclassicality in individual quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate semidefinite programs that serve as certificates and witnesses for nonclassicality, applicable to states, sources, measurements, and sets, and demonstrate them with examples.
result: They present explicit SDP-based methods that can certify nonclassicality in various scenarios, as illustrated by examples.
conclusion: The framework offers a versatile and computationally efficient approach to witness nonclassicality, advancing the study of quantum contextuality.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks, providing new lower bounds and a magic monotone.
motivation: To better understand and bound the stabilizer rank, a key resource in quantum computation, and to introduce new magic monotones.
method: The authors study the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states, derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define a new magic monotone (Barnes Wall norm), and provide a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They obtain the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which is best in the exponentially small fidelity regime, and show that the Barnes Wall norm is tightly upper bounded by T-count.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, offering new tools for quantum resource theory.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only partially understood for small tensor powers and qubit numbers. A complete theory is needed to unlock applications in pseudorandomness, learning, and entanglement distillation.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary tensor power and qubit number, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and develop a graphical calculus for manipulating these elements.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the theory to characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant provides a powerful tool for quantum information, with implications for magic state resource theories and property testing, and extends to prime-dimensional qudits.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

.
tldr: This paper presents a sample-optimal two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography using projected least squares, with rigorous error bounds and experimental validation on a superconducting quantum computer.
motivation: Quantum measurement tomography is essential for characterizing quantum devices, but existing protocols often have suboptimal sample complexity or high classical processing cost. The authors aim to design a protocol that is both sample-optimal and computationally efficient.
method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to measurement data from known probe states, then projects the unconstrained estimate onto the set of valid POVMs. They analyze sample complexity for worst-case and average-case distances, and establish matching lower bounds for any non-adaptive single-copy protocol.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both dimension and number of outcomes for both distance measures, with analytic forms for global and local 2-designs. Experiments on a noisy superconducting quantum computer confirm practical performance.
conclusion: The proposed projected least squares method is sample-optimal and computationally light, making it a practical and efficient solution for quantum measurement tomography, with broad applicability in quantum information processing.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security, with quadratic convergence of adversary success probability.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive. The authors aim to resolve this open problem.
method: They construct a specific scheme for an uncloneable bit and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and numerical computations, providing bounds on the adversary's success probability.
result: They prove the quadratic convergence bound for a range of key numbers and provide heuristic evidence for the general case, along with asymptotic and numerical upper bounds.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence for the feasibility of unconditional uncloneable encryption, advancing the theoretical foundations of quantum uncloneability.

title: Computational Bell Inequalities
authors: Ilya Merkulov And Rotem Arnon
abstract: We introduce a systematic approach for analyzing device-independent single-prover interactive protocols under computational assumptions. This is done by establishing an explicit correspondence with Bell inequalities and nonlocal games and constructing a computational space of correlations. We show how computational assumptions are converted to computational Bell inequalities, in their rigorous mathematical sense—a hyperplane that separates the sets of classical and quantum verifier-prover interactions. We reveal precisely how the nonsignaling assumption in standard device-independent setups admits a computational analogue through the challenge of learning a hidden input (which we define). We further utilize our fundamental results to study explicit protocols using the new perspective. We take advantage of modular tools for studying nonlocality, deriving tighter Tsirelson bounds for single-prover protocols and bounding the entropy generated in the interaction, improving on previous results. Our work thus establishes a modular approach to analyzing single-prover quantum certification protocols based on computational assumptions through the fundamental lens of Bell inequalities, removing many layers of technical overhead. The link that we draw between single-prover protocols and Bell inequalities goes far beyond the spread intuitive understanding or known results about ‘compiled nonlocal games’; Notably, it captures the exact way in which the correspondence between computational assumptions and locality should be understood also in protocols based on, e.g. trapdoor claw-free functions (in which there is no clear underlying nonlocal game).
tldr: This paper introduces computational Bell inequalities, establishing a rigorous correspondence between device-independent single-prover interactive protocols and Bell inequalities, and uses this to derive tighter Tsirelson bounds and entropy bounds.
motivation: To provide a modular and rigorous framework for analyzing device-independent protocols under computational assumptions, removing technical overhead and unifying with nonlocal games.
method: The authors construct a computational space of correlations and show how computational assumptions translate to hyperplanes separating classical and quantum interactions, analogous to Bell inequalities. They also define a computational analogue of nonsignaling via hidden input learning.
result: They derive tighter Tsirelson bounds for single-prover protocols and improve entropy generation bounds, demonstrating the utility of their framework on explicit protocols.
conclusion: The work establishes a fundamental link between single-prover quantum certification and Bell inequalities, offering a modular approach that extends beyond compiled nonlocal games and applies to protocols like trapdoor claw-free functions.

title: Gap Between Quantum Theory Based On Real And Complex Numbers Is Arbitrarily Large
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar, David Trillo, Marc Olivier Renou And Remigiusz Augusiak
abstract: Quantum information theory, the formalism for representing information contained in quantum systems, is based on complex Hilbert spaces. It was recently shown that in quantum networks involving three parties with nontrivial locality constraints, this formalism predicts correlations that cannot be explained by real quantum theory, a variant of quantum mechanics based on real Hilbert spaces. In this work, we study a scenario with parties sharing quantum systems in a star network. We then construct a multipartite Bell inequality that exhibits a gap between quantum theory and its variant based on real numbers, which grows linearly with , and is thus arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. This implies, that, as the number of parties grows, Hilbert space formalism based on real numbers becomes exceedingly worse at describing complex networks of quantum systems. We also compute the tolerance of this gap to experimental errors.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that the gap between real and complex quantum theory in a star network grows linearly with the number of parties, making it arbitrarily large.
motivation: Recent work showed that complex quantum theory is necessary to explain correlations in certain quantum networks, but the gap was small. This paper aims to show that the gap can be arbitrarily large, strengthening the case for complex Hilbert spaces.
method: The authors construct a multipartite Bell inequality for a star network with N parties and prove that the violation predicted by complex quantum theory grows linearly with N, while real quantum theory cannot exceed a constant bound.
result: The gap between real and complex quantum predictions increases linearly with the number of parties, becoming arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. They also compute the tolerance of this gap to experimental errors.
conclusion: The results imply that real quantum theory becomes increasingly inadequate for describing quantum networks as the number of parties grows, highlighting the fundamental role of complex numbers in quantum theory.

title: Modulator-Assisted Zeno Control Of Energy Transfer In Quantum Batteries
authors: Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, And Sabre Kais
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2178 (2026).

Efficient operation of quantum batteries requires not only fast energy transfer but also the ability to halt the charging process to prevent reverse flow. Existing approaches typically rely on direct control of the charger-battery interaction, which can be experimentally demanding. Here we propose a modulator-assisted quantum battery protocol that enables indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on. By applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, we exploit a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal three-body model and show that it remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit. We further extend the protocol to a collective many-body architecture, where it preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, scaling as [MATH] with the number of battery units. We also discuss a possible implementation in an NV-[MATH]C spin platform. Our results establish modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a modulator-assisted Zeno control protocol for quantum batteries, enabling indirect on/off switching of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on.
motivation: Efficient quantum battery operation requires halting charging to prevent reverse flow, but direct control of the charger-battery interaction is experimentally demanding. The authors aim to achieve indirect control using a modulator qubit.
method: They apply repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, exploiting a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. They analyze a minimal three-body model and extend to a collective many-body architecture.
result: The mechanism works beyond the ideal fast-control limit and preserves the collective charging power enhancement scaling with the number of battery units. They also discuss implementation in an NV-13C spin platform.
conclusion: Modulator-assisted Zeno control offers a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries, addressing a key challenge in quantum thermodynamics.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand whether the property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is robust to the choice of discrimination measure, which is fundamental for quantum state discrimination and its applications.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, and similar separation appears in multipartite cases for minimum-error but not unambiguous discrimination.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination measure in such studies.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to handle differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve dynamics, but standard NPO cannot directly handle differential constraints. The authors aim to bridge this gap to enable SDP-based bounds on time-evolved quantities.
method: They prove that any NPO problem with bounded operator variables satisfying ODEs can be transformed into an equivalent standard NPO problem, thus inheriting a complete SDP hierarchy. They then apply this to bound local observables in spin systems under Hamiltonian evolution.
result: The method yields tight bounds even in the thermodynamic limit for reasonably long evolution times, as demonstrated by low-level hierarchy approximations.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics via SDP relaxations, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics.

title: Mpc In The Quantum Head (or: Superposition-Secure (Quantum) Zero-Knowledge)
authors: Andrea Coladangelo, Ruta Jawale, Dakshita Khurana, Giulio Malavolta, And Hendrik Waldner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2161 (2026).

The MPC-in-the-head technique (Ishai et al., STOC 2007) is a celebrated method to build zero-knowledge protocols with desirable theoretical properties and high practical efficiency. This technique has generated a large body of research and has influenced the design of real-world post-quantum cryptographic signatures. In this work, we present a generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting, where the MPC is running a quantum computation. As an application of our framework, we propose a new approach to build zero-knowledge protocols where security holds even against a verifier that can obtain a superposition of transcripts. This notion was pioneered by Damgard et al., who built a zero-knowledge protocol for NP (in the common reference string model) secure against superposition attacks, by relying on perfectly hiding and unconditionally binding dual-mode commitments. Unfortunately, no such commitments are known from standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work we revisit this problem, and present two new three-round protocols in the common reference string model: (i) A zero-knowledge argument for NP, whose security reduces to the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem. (ii) A zero-knowledge argument for QMA from the same assumption.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes the MPC-in-the-head technique to the quantum setting, enabling zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks from standard LWE assumptions.
motivation: Existing zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks rely on dual-mode commitments that are not known from standard assumptions. The authors aim to construct such protocols from standard cryptographic assumptions.
method: They introduce a quantum generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm, where the MPC runs a quantum computation, and use it to build three-round zero-knowledge arguments in the common reference string model.
result: They present two protocols: one for NP and one for QMA, both secure against superposition attacks and based on the LWE assumption.
conclusion: This work provides a new framework for quantum zero-knowledge with practical implications for post-quantum cryptography, advancing the field of quantum information and cryptography.

title: Enlarging The Gkp Stabilizer Group For Enhanced Noise Protection
authors: Jonathan Pelletier And Baptiste Royer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2156 (2026).

Encoding a qubit in a larger Hilbert space of an oscillator is an efficient way to protect its quantum information against decoherence. Promising examples of such bosonic encodings are the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. In this work, we investigate how redefining the stabilizer group of the GKP codes to include all operations with trivial action on the code space can contribute to the search for an optimal implementation of a logical circuit when it is affected by noise. We find the generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group, allowing us to search for different physical implementations of a Clifford operation. We then propose an algorithm that finds the optimal implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, such that the state is less affected by loss errors during the computation. Finally, we demonstrate numerically, with logical randomized benchmarking, that such a compiler can increase the lifetime of square-GKP qubits while running Clifford circuits, compared to a random walk compiler.

.
tldr: This paper enlarges the GKP stabilizer group to include all operations with trivial action on the code space, enabling optimized Clifford circuit implementations that reduce loss errors and increase logical qubit lifetime.
motivation: GKP codes are promising for quantum error correction, but the standard stabilizer group may not capture all operations that preserve the code space. The authors aim to find optimal implementations of logical circuits under noise.
method: They derive the generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group and propose an algorithm to search for the optimal physical implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, minimizing loss errors during computation.
result: Numerical logical randomized benchmarking shows that their compiler increases the lifetime of square-GKP qubits running Clifford circuits compared to a random walk compiler.
conclusion: Redefining the stabilizer group to include all trivial-action operations provides a systematic way to optimize GKP circuits for noise protection, potentially improving fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Resourcefulness Of Non-classical Continuous-variable Quantum Gates
authors: Massimo Frigerio, Antoine Debray, Nicolas Treps, And Mattia Walschaers
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2155 (2026).

In continuous-variable quantum computation, identifying key elements that enable a quantum computational advantage is a long-standing issue. Starting from the standard results on the necessity of Wigner negativity, we develop a comprehensive and versatile approach in which the techniques of [MATH]-ordered quasiprobabilities are exploited to provide rigorous statements on the simulability of photonic quantum circuits consisting of previously characterized gates and thereby identifying the contribution of each quantum gate to the potential achievement of quantum computational advantage. This is achieved by means of an analysis of the so-called transfer function, allowing us to highlight the resourcefulness of a gate set. As such this technique can be straightforwardly applied to current continuous-variables quantum circuits, while also constraining the tolerable amount of losses above which any potential quantum advantage can be ruled out. We use [MATH]-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase-space to capture the non-classical features in the protocol, and focus our technique entirely on the ordering parameter [MATH]. This allows us to highlight the resourcefulness and robustness to loss of a universal set of unitary gates comprising three distinct Gaussian gates and any non-Gaussian unitary gate, providing important insight on the role of non-Gaussianity.

.
tldr: This paper develops a framework using s-ordered quasiprobabilities to analyze the resourcefulness of non-Gaussian gates in continuous-variable quantum computation, identifying conditions for quantum advantage and loss tolerance.
motivation: The paper aims to identify which quantum gates are essential for achieving quantum computational advantage in continuous-variable quantum computing, a long-standing open question.
method: The authors use s-ordered quasiprobability distributions and transfer functions to analyze the simulability of photonic circuits, focusing on the ordering parameter s to quantify non-classicality and resourcefulness of gate sets.
result: They show that a universal set of gates including Gaussian and any non-Gaussian unitary gate can be analyzed for resourcefulness and robustness to loss, providing bounds on tolerable losses for quantum advantage.
conclusion: The technique offers a practical tool for assessing the potential of continuous-variable quantum circuits and highlights the role of non-Gaussianity in achieving quantum advantage.

title: A Complexity Theory For Non-local Quantum Computation
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Simon Höfer, Alex May, Mikka Stasiuk, Philip Verduyn Lunel, And Henry Yuen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2152 (2026).

Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) replaces a local interaction between two systems with a single round of communication and shared entanglement. Despite many partial results, it is known that a characterization of entanglement cost in at least certain NLQC tasks would imply significant breakthroughs in complexity theory. Here, we avoid these obstructions and take an indirect approach to understanding resource requirements in NLQC, which mimics the approach used by complexity theorists: we study the relative hardness of different NLQC tasks by identifying resource efficient reductions between them. Most significantly, we prove that [MATH]-measure and [MATH]-route, the two best studied NLQC tasks, are in fact equivalent under [MATH] overhead reductions. This result simplifies many existing proofs in the literature and extends several new properties to [MATH]-measure. For instance, we obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on [MATH]-measure for all functions, and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class [MATH]. Beyond this, we study a number of other examples of NLQC tasks and their relationships.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complexity-theoretic framework for non-local quantum computation (NLQC), proving equivalences and reductions between NLQC tasks, and providing new upper bounds.
motivation: Characterizing the entanglement cost of NLQC tasks is known to be hard, so the authors take an indirect approach by studying relative hardness via reductions, mimicking complexity theory.
method: They define resource-efficient reductions between NLQC tasks and prove that two prominent tasks, [MATH]-measure and [MATH]-route, are equivalent under such reductions. They also analyze other NLQC tasks and their relationships.
result: They obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on [MATH]-measure for all functions and efficient protocols for functions in a certain complexity class, simplifying existing proofs and extending properties.
conclusion: The work provides a new perspective on NLQC resource requirements and establishes a complexity-theoretic framework that may guide future research.

title: Transducer Leakage Error Suppression Using Invariant-based Shortcut
authors: Shi-Qiang Qiao, Zheng Shan, Xue-Ke Song, Shi-Lei Su, Liu Ye And Dong Wang
abstract: We present a method for suppressing transducer leakage errors in spin-superconducting hybrid quantum systems with the theory of optimal invariant-based shortcut. By mediated virtual photons as a transducer to exchange the energy between the spin qubit and a transmon qubit, the fidelity of the population of the final state features a broad range above 99% under the influence of leakage error. The leakage probability from computational subspace to non-computational subspace can be effectively suppressed at a lowest value with . Based on the optimized pulse control designed by the invariant-based inverse engineering, the high-fidelity quantum iSWAP gate operations and entanglement state preparation within the computational subspace are achieved. Compared to the traditional pulse, derivative removal by adiabatic gate, counter-diabatic shortcut schemes, and limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno gradient ascent pulse engineering, the optimized shortcut scheme can still achieve a high fidelity with 99% in the presence of decoherence and control error. When taking into account the possibility of leakage errors in actual situations, our solution can still largely resist the influence of control errors. The results provides a feasible path for precisely manipulating the quantum state of hybrid quantum systems.
tldr: This paper proposes an invariant-based shortcut method to suppress transducer leakage errors in spin-superconducting hybrid quantum systems, achieving high-fidelity iSWAP gates and entanglement preparation.
motivation: Transducer leakage errors in hybrid quantum systems degrade gate fidelity, and existing pulse control methods are insufficient. The authors aim to develop a robust control scheme that suppresses leakage while maintaining high fidelity under realistic conditions.
method: They employ optimal invariant-based shortcut (inverse engineering) to design control pulses that minimize leakage from the computational subspace to non-computational states. They compare their approach with traditional pulses, DRAG, counter-diabatic shortcuts, and LBFGS gradient ascent pulse engineering.
result: The optimized shortcut scheme achieves population fidelities above 99% and effectively suppresses leakage probability to a minimal value, outperforming other methods in the presence of decoherence and control errors.
conclusion: The invariant-based shortcut provides a feasible and robust path for precise quantum state manipulation in hybrid quantum systems, particularly for suppressing transducer leakage errors.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical color codes under measurement-biased noise, introducing the teraquop volume metric and showing that belief matching decoding can significantly improve performance.
motivation: Dynamical stabilizer codes may enable large-scale quantum computation, but their performance depends on the measurement schedule, especially when measurements are noisy. The authors aim to optimize schedules for hardware with noisy readouts.
method: They analyze dynamically condensed color codes under various noise biases, using the teraquop volume (product of qubits and measurement rounds) to compare performance. They test repeating measurements and compare belief matching with minimum-weight perfect matching decoders.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance under measurement-biased noise but offers little benefit for unbiased or X-biased noise. The teraquop volume reveals that differences are mainly due to measurement rounds, not qubit count. Belief matching can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one.
conclusion: The teraquop volume is a valuable metric for comparing codes, and correlated-error decoding is crucial for optimizing dynamical codes under realistic noise.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute non-Clifford quantum error correction circuits, using Shor's algorithm for factoring 21 as a case study.
motivation: To identify the critical requirements for the control and decoding hardware needed to run fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, specifically non-Clifford circuits, which are a key milestone for quantum advantage.
method: The authors convert a logical-level Shor's algorithm circuit for factoring 21 into a surface code circuit and then to a physical-level circuit, incorporating realistic superconducting qubit parameters and simulating the full fault-tolerant circuit.
result: They find that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data among multiple decoders with fast communication, and that near-term hardware with ~0.1% error rates and ~1000 qubits is sufficient.
conclusion: The requirements outlined provide a roadmap for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits, guiding the development of control and decoding systems.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

.
tldr: This paper determines the optimal T-count for approximating arbitrary quantum states and diagonal unitaries, showing that ancilla qubits allow for asymptotically optimal scaling.
motivation: The number of T gates is a critical resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and understanding the minimal T-count for state preparation is fundamental for efficient quantum algorithms.
method: The authors improve prior work by Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, providing constructive algorithms and lower bounds to establish the optimal asymptotic scaling of T-count for state preparation and diagonal unitary synthesis.
result: They show that the optimal T-count for approximating an arbitrary n-qubit state to error epsilon is Theta(2^n + log(1/epsilon)) when ancilla qubits are allowed, and similarly for diagonal unitaries. They also demonstrate parallel synthesis of many single-qubit unitaries for the price of one.
conclusion: The work settles the asymptotic T-count complexity for state preparation and diagonal unitaries, offering practical implications for quantum circuit optimization and resource estimation.

title: Resource Quantification For Programming Low-depth Quantum Circuits
authors: Entong He And Yuxiang Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2166 (2026).

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices pave the way for implementing quantum algorithms that offer quantum advantages over their classical counterparts. Due to the intrinsic noise and decoherence in the physical system, NISQ machines are naturally modeled as large-scale, low-depth quantum circuits. In practice, executing such circuits requires sending program states that encode the relevant instructions to a programmable quantum computer, typically through a cloud service. Existing programming approaches designed for generic unitary transformations are computationally inefficient in the low-depth setting, and therefore remain unsatisfactory. As such, to realize NISQ algorithms, it is crucial to find an efficient way to program low-depth circuits as the number of qubits [MATH] increases. Here, we investigate the circuit complexity and the size of quantum memory, known as the program cost, required to program low-depth brickwork circuits. We establish a tight worst-case program cost of [MATH] for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-[MATH] regime. Moreover, we analyze the trade-off between the cost of describing the layout of local gates and the cost of programming them to implement the target unitaries via the light-cone argument. Our findings suggest that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.

.
tldr: This paper studies the resource cost (program size and circuit complexity) for programming low-depth brickwork quantum circuits, establishing a tight worst-case program cost and analyzing trade-offs.
motivation: Efficiently programming NISQ devices is crucial for practical quantum advantage, but existing methods for generic unitaries are inefficient for low-depth circuits.
method: The authors analyze the circuit complexity and quantum memory size required to program low-depth brickwork circuits, using light-cone arguments to trade off layout description cost and programming cost.
result: They establish a tight worst-case program cost for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-qubit regime, and show that gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
conclusion: The findings provide fundamental resource bounds for programming low-depth quantum circuits, guiding the design of efficient programming strategies for NISQ devices.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations (CZ-complexity) needed to prepare graph states, relating it to rank-width and providing algorithms for interval and circle graphs.
motivation: Understanding the resource cost of preparing graph states is crucial for quantum information processing, as graph states are key resources for measurement-based quantum computing and quantum error correction.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and provide a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and edge-complementations. They then relate CZ-complexity to rank-width and develop preparation algorithms for specific graph classes.
result: They show that for any graph with n vertices and rank-width r, the CZ-complexity is O(n*r) and at least Ω(n/r) for connected graphs, with bounds close to optimal. They also give algorithms with CZ-complexity O(n) for interval graphs and O(n log n) for circle graphs.
conclusion: The work provides a deeper understanding of the complexity of graph-state preparation, offering both lower and upper bounds and efficient algorithms for certain graph families, which may inform practical quantum circuit optimization.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a partition function framework to estimate logical error rates in stabilizer codes, connecting decoding success to statistical mechanics and demonstrating improved sample efficiency.
motivation: Accurate estimation of logical error rates is crucial for assessing quantum error correction performance, but direct simulation of decoders can be inefficient, especially at low noise.
method: The authors define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to maximum likelihood decoding and an order probability for a probabilistic decoder, mapping to disordered statistical mechanics models. They analyze the toric code under bitflip noise and the color code under various noise models.
result: They show that estimating decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than counting decoder failures, and discuss the possibility of a decodability boundary distinct from the order-disorder phase boundary. Ensembling remains useful even when noise lifts degeneracy.
conclusion: The partition function approach provides a powerful tool for estimating logical error rates and understanding decoding strategies, with implications for optimizing quantum error correction.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: This paper introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a new characterization of robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements, proving it necessary and sufficient and computable in polynomial time.
motivation: Pauli Flow was previously shown to be insufficient for characterizing determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, and the authors aim to provide a complete characterization.
method: The authors define Shadow Pauli Flow as an extension of Pauli Flow and prove that an MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow, also providing a polynomial-time algorithm.
result: They demonstrate that Pauli flow is necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense, but Shadow Pauli Flow is necessary and sufficient in full generality, and can be computed in polynomial time.
conclusion: Shadow Pauli Flow provides a complete and efficient characterization of determinism in MBQCs with Pauli measurements, advancing the theory of measurement-based quantum computing.

title: From Superradiance To Superabsorption: An Exact Treatment Of Non-Markovian Cooperative Radiation
authors: Ignacio González And Ángel Rivas
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2159 (2026).

We investigate the emergence of cooperative radiation phenomena in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy resonant cavity beyond the Markovian and mean-field approximations. By deriving a complete analytical solution for the two-emitter case and employing a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, we characterize the full transition from Markovian to non-Markovian collective dynamics for systems of up to [MATH] emitters. Our results reveal three distinct regimes: a Markovian phase exhibiting the standard superradiant burst, a non-Markovian phase featuring spontaneous superabsorption of the emitted field, and a critical regime marked by pulsed collective emission. We show that the critical spectral width separating these behaviors increases monotonically with the number of emitters, demonstrating that environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity. Finally, we find that the superradiant scaling of the peak intensity progressively degrades with increasing system size, approaching a subquadratic law in the limit of a perfect cavity. In this regime, spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct manifestation of non-Markovian cooperativity.

.
tldr: This paper provides an exact analytical and numerical treatment of cooperative radiation in two-level atoms coupled to a lossy cavity, revealing non-Markovian superabsorption and a degradation of superradiant scaling with system size.
motivation: To understand cooperative radiation beyond Markovian and mean-field approximations, which is crucial for quantum information processing with spin ensembles in cavities.
method: Derives a complete analytical solution for two emitters and uses a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, characterizing the transition from Markovian to non-Markovian dynamics.
result: Identifies three regimes: Markovian superradiance, non-Markovian superabsorption, and critical pulsed emission; shows that the critical spectral width increases with emitter number and that superradiant scaling degrades to subquadratic in the perfect cavity limit.
conclusion: Environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity, and spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct non-Markovian cooperative phenomenon, with implications for quantum memory and light-matter interfaces.

title: Constrained Quantum Optimization Via Iterative Warm-start X Y ...
authors: David Bucher, Maximilian Janetschek, Michael Poppel, Jonas Stein, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien And Sebastian Feld
abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a leading hybrid heuristic for combinatorial optimization, but efficiently handling hard constraints remains a significant challenge. -mixers successfully confine quantum state evolution to a feasible subspace, such as the Hamming-weight-1 sector for one-hot constraints. On the contrary, warm-starting biases the search toward promising regions based on preliminary solutions. Combining these two techniques requires maintaining the essential alignment between the initial state and the mixer Hamiltonian to preserve convergence guarantees. Previous work demonstrated warm-starting with -mixers via a biased initial state, but relying only on standard mixer Hamiltonians. Consequently, the initial state is no longer a ground state of the mixer. In this work, we overcome these limitations by formulating a warm-started -mixer Hamiltonian for one-hot constraints and proving its ground-state properties. Furthermore, we provide a shallow circuit implementation suitable for NISQ implementations. We embed the warm-starting into a classical heuristic that iteratively updates the bias based on previous samples, called iterative warm-starting (IWS). Extensive numerical simulations on Max- -Cut and traveling salesperson problem instances demonstrate that IWS-QAOA significantly accelerates the solution-finding process, increasing the probability of sampling optimal solutions by orders of magnitude compared to standard XY-QAOA. Finally, we validate our approach on the ibm_boston QPU using hardware-tailored 144-qubit problem instances. By coupling IWS-QAOA with a greedy steepest-descent post-processing strategy to repair infeasible measurements caused by hardware noise, we successfully identify optimal solutions on actual quantum devices.
tldr: This paper introduces a warm-started XY-mixer for QAOA to handle one-hot constraints, proving ground-state properties and demonstrating significant speedups in finding optimal solutions on both simulations and a 144-qubit IBM quantum processor.
motivation: QAOA struggles with hard constraints, and existing warm-starting methods with XY-mixers lose convergence guarantees. The authors aim to combine warm-starting with XY-mixers while preserving the initial state as a ground state of the mixer.
method: They formulate a warm-started XY-mixer Hamiltonian for one-hot constraints, prove its ground-state properties, and provide a shallow circuit implementation. They embed this in an iterative warm-starting (IWS) heuristic that updates biases based on previous samples.
result: Numerical simulations on Max-k-Cut and TSP instances show IWS-QAOA increases the probability of sampling optimal solutions by orders of magnitude compared to standard XY-QAOA. Hardware experiments on ibm_boston with 144 qubits, combined with post-processing, successfully find optimal solutions.
conclusion: The proposed warm-started XY-mixer and iterative warm-starting significantly enhance QAOA's performance on constrained optimization problems, making it more practical for NISQ devices.

title: Security Of Binary-modulated Optical Key Distribution Against Quantum-enhanced Coherent Eavesdropping
authors: Karol Łukanowski, Michał Wójcik, Stefano Olivares, Konrad Banaszek And Marcin Jarzyna
abstract: Optical key distribution protects the physical layer of communication links by taking advantage of the inherent noise present in the photodetection process. It allows for efficient generation of a shared random key between two distant users that is secure against passive eavesdropping and can be subsequently used for cryptographic purposes. Moreover, it can be straightforwardly implemented over standard intensity modulation and direct detection links, making it an attractive alternative to quantum key distribution. Here we present a comprehensive security analysis against more powerful eavesdroppers possessing the ability to perform either coherent detection, or even quantum-optimal measurements on the intercepted transmission.
tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive security analysis of binary-modulated optical key distribution against quantum-enhanced coherent eavesdropping, showing its robustness against powerful adversaries.
motivation: Optical key distribution (OKD) is a practical alternative to QKD, but its security against advanced quantum eavesdropping was not fully characterized. The authors aim to assess its security under coherent and quantum-optimal measurements.
method: The authors analyze the security of binary-modulated OKD by considering eavesdroppers with coherent detection and quantum-optimal measurements, deriving key rate bounds and comparing them to standard QKD.
result: The analysis shows that OKD remains secure against these advanced attacks, with key rates that are competitive with QKD under certain conditions, though quantum-optimal measurements reduce performance.
conclusion: Binary-modulated OKD offers a viable and secure alternative to QKD, even against quantum-enhanced eavesdropping, making it attractive for practical deployment.

title: Hoare Meets Heisenberg: A Lightweight Logic For Quantum Programs
authors: Aarthi Sundaram, Robert Rand, Kartik Singhal, Youngchan Cho, And Brad Lackey
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2172 (2026).

We show that Gottesman's (1998) semantics for Clifford circuits based on the Heisenberg representation gives rise to a lightweight Hoare-like logic for efficiently characterizing a common subset of quantum programs. Our applications include (i) certifying whether auxiliary qubits can be safely disposed of, (ii) determining if a system is separable across a given bipartition, (iii) checking the transversality of a gate with respect to a given stabilizer code, and (iv) computing post-measurement states for computational basis measurements. Further, this logic is extended to accommodate universal quantum computing by deriving Hoare triples for the [MATH]-gate, multiply-controlled unitaries such as the Toffoli gate, and some gate injection circuits that use associated magic states. A number of interesting results emerge from this logic, including a lower bound on the number of [MATH] gates necessary to perform a multiply-controlled [MATH] gate.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a lightweight Hoare-like logic for quantum programs based on Gottesman's Heisenberg semantics, enabling efficient certification of properties like qubit disposal, separability, and transversality.
motivation: To provide a practical, lightweight verification method for quantum programs, especially those using Clifford circuits and stabilizer codes, without the complexity of full quantum program logics.
method: The authors formalize a Hoare logic using the Heisenberg representation of Clifford circuits, deriving rules for common operations and extending to universal quantum computing via magic states and Toffoli gates.
result: The logic enables efficient certification of auxiliary qubit disposal, bipartite separability, gate transversality, and post-measurement states, and yields a lower bound on T-gates for multiply-controlled gates.
conclusion: The proposed logic offers a practical tool for quantum program verification, with potential applications in quantum error correction and resource management.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error-correction performance and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and constructing efficient quantum LDPC codes with good performance is a key challenge.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, derive from classical QC-LDPC codes, and propose an encoding scheme exploiting the code structure. They also use a quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum decoder.
result: The proposed codes achieve nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance compared to layered binary sum-product decoding, and show significant improvements over prior works under depolarizing and Markovian noise.
conclusion: The constructions are scalable and resource-efficient, making them promising for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, addressing time-optimal, noisy, and dual-species scenarios.
motivation: As neutral atom quantum processors scale to thousands of atoms, robust rearrangement algorithms are needed, but existing work lacks open-source tools and noise considerations.
method: The authors develop the atommovr simulation framework and use it to benchmark rearrangement algorithms under noiseless and noisy conditions, including a novel dual-species algorithm called InsideOut.
result: They extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identify advantageous strategies across error regimes, and demonstrate that InsideOut avoids blocked configurations with near-unity success.
conclusion: The framework provides a common tool for the community to study and improve atom rearrangement, lowering the barrier for experimental groups and stimulating algorithm development.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits using tensor network contraction and Markov processes, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of large quantum circuits is limited by exponential overhead, and approximate methods are often insufficient. The authors aim to provide an exact sampling method that scales to hundreds of qubits, enabling validation of quantum algorithms and conjectures at larger scales.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. It is designed to sample from ideal and noisy circuits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models.
result: The method successfully generates samples from QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, including noisy cases, demonstrating scalability beyond previous exact simulation capabilities.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation for quantum algorithm research, providing a tool to test assumptions and conjectures at scales previously inaccessible.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to find schedules that minimize convergence time for solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare target states via frequent measurements, but multi-channel versions with non-commuting observables are not well understood. The authors aim to provide a theoretical foundation and optimize the dragging schedule for practical quantum information tasks.
method: They derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and use optimal control theory to find schedules that lower-bound convergence time in low-dimensional settings.
result: They obtain analytical bounds and optimal schedules that improve convergence time compared to naive approaches, demonstrated on k-SAT examples.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical basis for multi-channel Zeno dragging and offers guidance for designing optimal schedules for measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture on geometric speed limits for state preparation, showing that extrinsic curvature of control spaces can lead to violations.
motivation: The authors aim to test a conjecture that energy fluctuations during state preparation are lower bounded by the minimal geometric length of accessible protocols, which would provide fundamental limits on quantum control.
method: They analyze the conjecture using qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems, demonstrating counterexamples where the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature.
result: The conjecture is violated in systems with curved control spaces, indicating that geometric length alone does not bound energy fluctuations.
conclusion: The geometric speed limit conjecture is not universally valid; extrinsic curvature must be considered in quantum control and thermodynamics.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem.
